evaluation.positioning_hook: After her ex-boyfriend is murdered at school, Macy digs into a buried teen death and discovers the girl everyone thought was dead may be hunting her classmates.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is immediately legible to YA and genre buyers: a popular teen murder, a school setting, and a buried past crime that turns supernatural. It has clear binge appeal, though the teen-skew and horror turn narrow it more than a broad four-quadrant play.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The pilot lands its engine by the auditorium reveal and then sharpens it with the Lillian Crawford thread and the warehouse kill. The opening limo attack is striking, but the script takes a while to clarify whether this is a murder mystery, ghost story, or slasher-adjacent teen thriller.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Macy has a clean emotional engine — grief, guilt, and a need to find out what happened — and the friend group gives her a social world to push against. The supporting teens are functional but still mostly archetypes in this draft, so the long-term character draw is more centered on Macy than on a fully differentiated ensemble.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The school-assembly murder reveal and the final warehouse attack give the pilot a strong genre swing, and the Lillian Crawford mythology hints at a bigger engine. The execution leans familiar in its teen-drama surfaces and dialogue rhythms, so the boldness is more in premise than in voice.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The pilot moves efficiently from Ryan’s attack to the school announcement to Macy’s private investigation and then to the final kill. There is a real escalation pattern, though several early scenes spend time establishing social texture before the central mystery fully locks in.

resonant_originality.reasoning: A murdered ex-boyfriend, a dead girl from the past, and a final reveal of the killer in the shadows is a solid genre combination, but it still sits near familiar teen-thriller territory. The school-wide public grief scene and the possible supernatural return of Lillian are the freshest elements.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The high school, wealthy neighborhood, and friend-group hierarchy are clear, but the world mostly functions as a container for the mystery rather than a fully rule-driven ecosystem. The Lillian Crawford history suggests deeper mythology, yet the pilot only begins to sketch those rules.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a consistent eerie, mournful register, especially in the auditorium sequence and Macy’s night research scene. At the same time, the opening’s glossy teen banter and the later horror beats feel adjacent rather than fully fused into a singular tonal signature.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The Lillian Crawford file, the closed police report, and the suggestion that the past is still active all imply a larger mythology beneath the pilot. That gives the series room to deepen into institutional cover-up, inherited guilt, or supernatural rules if the show keeps paying off the breadcrumbs.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Macy’s friend group gives the pilot a usable social engine, and the Ryan absence creates immediate relational pressure inside the ensemble. But the relationships are still mostly defined by function — confidant, skeptic, jokester, popular girl — rather than by sharply distinct interpersonal agendas.

lead_characters.name: Macy
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 16-17, high-school student, affluent suburban setting.
lead_characters.hook: Macy is the social-center teen who performs confidence for everyone around her, then collapses into guilt and obsession when Ryan is murdered and she realizes she may have missed the warning signs. She becomes the pilot’s engine the moment grief turns into investigation, and her emotional contradiction — polished, funny, and outwardly in control while privately unraveling — gives the role real series durability.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Katherine Langford in 13 Reasons Why — a lead who can carry grief, anger, and private unraveling while still holding the room. It gives an actor the rare teen-drama combination of emotional breakdown, sleuthing momentum, and moral intensity.

lead_characters.name: Jessica
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late teens, high-school student, socially polished.
lead_characters.hook: Jessica is the polished friend who reads as supportive, stylish, and socially fluent, but she also functions as the group’s pressure valve and emotional translator. She’s the kind of character who can either stay a confidante or become a sharper source of tension as the mystery deepens.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Shay Mitchell in Pretty Little Liars a lane — glamorous, watchable, and always carrying a second thought behind the smile. It offers an actor a chance to play social ease with just enough ambiguity to keep viewers leaning in.

lead_characters.name: Kyle
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late teens, high-school student, popular athlete type.
lead_characters.hook: Kyle is the smirking, self-aware alpha in the friend group, the one who jokes to keep the mood light but still registers the danger when the school’s social order starts cracking. He reads as a classic teen ensemble power player, with enough charisma to matter if the show wants a male peer who can pivot from comic relief to suspect.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This has the easy, scene-stealing confidence of a Noah Centineo-type teen role in its early phase, but with more room for suspicion and fear. It gives an actor the chance to play charm first and then let the mask slip.

lead_characters.name: Nina
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-to-late teens, high-school student, sharp-tongued.
lead_characters.hook: Nina is the sarcastic observer who cuts through the group’s performative confidence and keeps the banter moving. She’s useful because she can deliver exposition, skepticism, and social commentary without losing the teen texture of the show.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of sharp supporting part that made Lili Reinhart’s early Riverdale work pop — dry, readable, and always one beat away from revealing something deeper. It gives an actor a reliable mix of wit and vulnerability in a genre ensemble.

lead_characters.name: Ethan
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late teens, high-school student, jokester-athlete type.
lead_characters.hook: Ethan is the easygoing comic presence who keeps the group from feeling too heavy, but the pilot also gives him a nervous edge once Ryan’s death and the Lillian talk surface. He’s the kind of supporting character who can become more interesting if the show lets the humor conceal real fear.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the sort of role that lets an actor do the Tyler Posey-in-Teen Wolf job: likable, fast, and emotionally accessible, with room to turn serious when the genre darkens. It’s a good showcase for timing and for a later reveal of vulnerability.

lead_characters.name: Alex
lead_characters.hook: Alex appears as a secondary teen with knowledge of the danger, then reappears in the warehouse sequence as the next victim, which makes her more of a plot function than a fully built character in this draft. Still, she signals that the show is willing to widen the danger beyond Macy’s immediate circle.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of brief but memorable genre role that can give an actor a strong fear-and-urgency showcase, similar to the early victims in Scream-style teen horror. It’s a compact opportunity to make a mark fast.

lead_characters.name: Ryan
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 17, high-school student, ex-boyfriend, murder victim.
lead_characters.hook: Ryan is the absent center of the pilot: a smug, charismatic teen whose death detonates the story and whose memory keeps driving Macy’s guilt. He’s more catalyst than active character here, but the script uses him effectively as the emotional wound that the mystery keeps reopening.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor a memorable opening and then a powerful afterimage, like the dead-boyfriend catalyst parts in teen mystery shows. The showcase is in making the audience feel the loss before the plot even begins.

lead_characters.name: Lillian Crawford
lead_characters.demographics: Female, teen at time of death, deceased or possibly alive depending on series mythology.
lead_characters.hook: Lillian is the mythic past event the pilot keeps circling: a dead teen whose unresolved death may be connected to Ryan’s murder and who may not actually be gone. She’s the series’ most obvious mythology hook, and the script smartly leaves her as a rumor, a file, and a threat rather than over-explaining her too early.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of eerie, high-concept mythology role that can become a breakout if the show reveals her in a way that redefines the series, similar to the mystery-presence characters in prestige teen horror. It gives an actor the chance to play legend, menace, and possibly tragedy.

lead_characters.name: Principal Hawthorne
lead_characters.hook: Principal Hawthorne is the institutional face of the pilot’s public grief, the adult who has to stand in front of the school and say the unsayable. He functions as a pressure valve for the school setting and a reminder that the story has adult systems around it, even if the teens are driving the action.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of authority role that lets a veteran character actor land one of the pilot’s biggest public scenes, similar to the principal/administrator parts in prestige teen dramas. The showcase is controlled authority cracking under pressure.

lead_characters.name: Sheriff Sanders
lead_characters.hook: Sheriff Sanders arrives as the ominous adult voice of suspicion, framing the murder as a community-wide trust problem and hinting that the past matters. She’s a useful genre authority figure because she can either be ally, obstacle, or keeper of the buried truth.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene-setting authority role that gives an actor a strong monologue and instant presence, like the law-enforcement figures in small-town mystery pilots. It offers gravitas and a chance to control the room.

lead_characters.name: Mom
lead_characters.hook: Mom is the warm domestic counterweight to the pilot’s dread, the person trying to keep the house normal while Macy spirals inward. She gives the series a grounded family anchor and a place for emotional fallout to land.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of parent role that lets an actor do the emotional support work that made Connie Britton-style teen-drama parents so memorable. The showcase is quiet authority and protective warmth.

lead_characters.name: Dad
lead_characters.hook: Dad is the calm, lightly comic household presence who helps establish the pilot’s normal before the mystery tears through it. He’s not deeply defined yet, but he helps sell the cost of the story on the family level.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of understated parent role that gives a seasoned actor a chance to ground the show without overplaying it. The showcase is subtle domestic realism.

lead_characters.name: Gabby
lead_characters.hook: Gabby is the younger sibling who keeps the home scenes alive and gives Macy someone innocent to protect. He also functions as a useful witness to the hooded figure outside the house, which makes him more than just comic relief.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a clean child supporting role with a little mystery utility, similar to the younger-sibling parts that often become audience favorites in teen thrillers. It gives a young actor a chance to be funny, observant, and vulnerable.

lead_characters.name: Mia
lead_characters.hook: Mia is a small but functional peer character who helps widen the school ecosystem beyond Macy’s immediate circle. She’s currently more texture than engine, but she contributes to the sense that the school has multiple social lanes running at once.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting teen role that gives an actor a clean, believable school-world presence without needing to carry the plot. It’s a useful ensemble credit with room to grow.

possible stunt/double needs for the opening limo attack and warehouse kill

notable_requirements: limo interior and street exterior for opening attack

technical.vfx_details: Mostly practical horror coverage with possible enhancement for the limo crash, tire burst, and a few supernatural shadow/motion beats around Lillian.
technical.sfx_needs: Blood effects, vehicle impact coverage, practical injury makeup, and controlled violence for the opening attack and warehouse kill.

rights_flags.detail: "Happier Than Ever" by Billie Eilish is used in the opening limo sequence.
"When the Party's Over" by Billie Eilish is used in the auditorium and bedroom sequences.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Serialized teen mystery-horror with a case-of-the-past engine: each episode can advance the Ryan/Lillian investigation while delivering a new threat or reveal.

budget.note: Contemporary school, home, and warehouse settings keep the footprint contained, but the opening limo attack, night exteriors, and recurring music clearances add cost pressure.

casting.note: The project lives or dies on a teen lead who can play grief, suspicion, and determination without losing likability, plus a credible teen ensemble around her.

development.note: The pilot clearly sets up Macy, Ryan, and Lillian, but the show still has to define how far the mystery leans supernatural versus grounded murder investigation.

comp_set.title: Pretty Little Liars
comp_set.why_it_comps: Teen social hierarchy, buried secrets, and a female-led mystery engine built around a dead or missing figure.

comp_set.title: Riverdale
comp_set.why_it_comps: High-school melodrama fused with murder mystery and a heightened, ominous undercurrent.

comp_set.title: Scream
comp_set.why_it_comps: Teen ensemble horror language, public-school danger, and a killer who turns social spaces into threat zones.

comp_set.title: Teen Wolf
comp_set.why_it_comps: Serialized teen genre storytelling with a school setting, friend-group engine, and escalating supernatural menace.

audience_target.primary_audience: Teen and young-adult genre viewers who want school-set mystery, grief-driven stakes, and a strong female lead.
audience_target.demographics: Primarily F16-34, with secondary male teen/young-adult reach; strongest among viewers who already watch YA mystery, horror, and supernatural serials.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary teen ensemble with mostly practical violence, school/home locations, and a few night exterior set pieces; assume an 8-episode season.

types_of_buyers: genre-forward development execs building female-led mystery lanes
indie TV producers looking for contained supernatural series
lane_fit.detail: The script sits naturally in the school-mystery lane: female lead, social-circle pressure, a dead teen, and a possible supernatural return. It is built for bingeable streaming rather than broadcast procedural repetition.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone series engine at present; no clear spinoff vector beyond the core Macy/Lillian mystery.

strengths.what_it_means: This is the kind of public, communal shock scene that gives a buyer an immediate trailer moment and a clear emotional promise. It will attract streamers and genre producers looking for a pilot that announces its stakes in one room, one speech, and one devastating turn.
strengths.evidence: Principal Hawthorne announces Ryan’s murder in front of the entire school while the Billie Eilish cue underscores the collapse of normalcy.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Macy has a usable grief engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead is not just reacting to a mystery; she is personally implicated, which gives the series emotional propulsion beyond case-of-the-week mechanics. That makes the role attractive to actors and to buyers who want a female-led hook with built-in obsession.
strengths.evidence: Macy’s guilt over not answering Ryan’s calls becomes the emotional trigger for her investigation and refusal to let the death go.

strengths.what_it_means: The old police report and school archive material give the series a second-layer engine that can expand beyond the pilot murder. Buyers respond to mythology that can deepen over time without needing to reinvent the premise every episode.
strengths.evidence: Macy finds the 2008 Lillian Crawford death file, the closed investigation, and the old newspaper headlines tying the past to the present.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The final warehouse kill promises escalation.
strengths.what_it_means: Ending on a fresh murder confirms the show is not just a grief drama but an active danger engine, which helps the pilot feel like the start of a series rather than a one-off mystery. That kind of closing beat is useful for retention and for signaling genre commitment to buyers.
strengths.evidence: Alex follows the lead into the abandoned warehouse and is attacked by the cloaked figure, revealed as Lillian.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, bingeable teen mystery-horror package: a female lead with a personal wound, a school-wide murder reveal, and a buried past that can keep generating episodes. The contemporary locations and mostly practical violence keep it in a buyer-friendly indie TV lane, while the public grief set piece and final kill give it the kind of trailer moments streamers can market fast.

items.area: The genre identity is still split.
items.detail: The pilot opens like glossy teen drama, pivots into murder mystery, and then lands on overt horror/supernatural imagery with Lillian in the warehouse. That blend can work, but buyers will want to know whether the series is primarily grounded investigation or full supernatural thriller before they commit.

items.area: The supporting teens read as archetypes.
items.detail: Jessica, Kyle, Nina, and Ethan each have a clear function in the group, but the pilot mostly gives them social flavor rather than distinct agendas. That keeps the ensemble usable, but it also means the show is still heavily dependent on Macy carrying the emotional and narrative load.

"Happier Than Ever" and "When the Party's Over" are both named and used as emotional punctuation, which means the pilot is carrying real sync cost and approval risk. Those cues are doing work on the page, but they are also the kind of named-music asks that business affairs will flag immediately.

items.area: The pilot leans on familiar teen-thriller grammar.
items.detail: The popular school clique, the dead boyfriend, the secret past, and the creepy figure in black are all effective, but they sit close to well-worn genre language. That makes the hook accessible, but it also means the series will need a sharper signature in later episodes to separate from the field.

issues.headline: The main buyer conversation is genre definition: the pilot wants to be teen drama, murder mystery, and supernatural horror at once, and that ambiguity will shape the pitch. The other friction points are familiar but real — an ensemble still in archetype mode and two named Billie Eilish tracks that add immediate clearance work.
